note: wordPartClue is what the parts literally suggest. studentDefinition and scienceExplanation are the actual science meaning. They are kept separate on purpose: the clue opens the door, the science confirms the meaning.

terms.studentDefinition: The study of living things.
terms.scienceExplanation: Biology is the science of living things — how they are built, how they grow, what they need, and how they interact.
terms.contextExample: A biologist studying a pond records which plants and animals live there and what each one needs to survive.

terms.studentDefinition: The study of Earth and its rocks.
terms.scienceExplanation: Geology is the science of Earth's materials and the processes that change them, including rocks, soil, and the layers below the surface.
terms.contextExample: A geologist reads the layers in a canyon wall to work out which rock formed first.

terms.wordPartClue: home or surroundings + the study of
terms.studentDefinition: The study of how living things interact with their surroundings.
terms.scienceExplanation: Ecology examines the relationships between organisms and the living and nonliving parts of the place where they live.
terms.contextExample: Studying how a drought changes which animals stay in a prairie is ecology.

terms.studentDefinition: All of Earth's water.
terms.scienceExplanation: The hydrosphere is all the water on Earth — oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater, ice, and water vapor in the air.
terms.contextExample: Oceans, lakes, groundwater, glaciers, and water vapor are all part of the hydrosphere.

terms.wordPartClue: vapor or air + region or layer
terms.studentDefinition: The layer of gases that surrounds Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: The atmosphere is the mixture of gases held around Earth by gravity. It holds the air we breathe, carries weather, and blocks some of the Sun's energy.
terms.contextExample: Clouds form in the atmosphere when water vapor cools and condenses.

terms.studentDefinition: All the places on Earth where living things are found.
terms.scienceExplanation: The biosphere is every part of Earth where life exists, from deep ocean water to soil to the lower atmosphere.
terms.contextExample: Bacteria living in desert soil and fish living near the ocean floor are both part of the biosphere.

terms.studentDefinition: The rock and soil part of Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: The geosphere is Earth's solid material — surface rock and soil, and the layers of rock and metal beneath.
terms.contextExample: A landslide moves material from one part of the geosphere to another.

terms.studentDefinition: A tool used to measure temperature.
terms.scienceExplanation: A thermometer measures temperature, which tells how hot or cold something is. Scientists use it to collect data they can compare.
terms.contextExample: Students used a thermometer to record the water temperature every ten minutes.

terms.studentDefinition: A tool that measures how fast something is moving.
terms.scienceExplanation: A speedometer reports speed — the distance an object travels in a certain amount of time.
terms.contextExample: The speedometer showed the car traveling 30 miles per hour.

terms.studentDefinition: A tool for looking at very small things.
terms.scienceExplanation: A microscope uses lenses to make small objects look larger, so scientists can observe details the eye cannot see alone.
terms.contextExample: Under a microscope, a drop of pond water is full of moving organisms.

terms.studentDefinition: A tool for looking at things that are very far away.
terms.scienceExplanation: A telescope gathers light from distant objects so they appear brighter and larger, which is how we observe planets and stars.
terms.contextExample: Through a telescope, the four largest moons of Jupiter look like tiny points of light in a line.

terms.studentDefinition: Too small to see without a microscope.
terms.scienceExplanation: Microscopic describes an object so small that a microscope is needed to observe it.
terms.contextExample: The leaf has microscopic openings that let gases move in and out.

terms.studentDefinition: Large enough to see without a microscope.
terms.scienceExplanation: Macroscopic describes something you can observe with your eyes alone.
terms.contextExample: The salt crystals were macroscopic, but the dissolved salt in the water was not visible at all.

terms.studentDefinition: The process plants use to make their own food using light.
terms.scienceExplanation: In photosynthesis, plants use energy from sunlight together with water and carbon dioxide to make sugar, and they release oxygen.
terms.contextExample: A plant kept in a dark closet for two weeks turns pale and stops growing well.

terms.wordPartClue: home or surroundings + parts working together
terms.studentDefinition: All the living and nonliving things in one place, working together.
terms.scienceExplanation: An ecosystem includes organisms and the nonliving parts of their environment — water, air, soil, sunlight — and the interactions among them.
terms.contextExample: A pond ecosystem includes fish, insects, algae, water, mud, and sunlight.

terms.studentDefinition: A living thing too small to see without a microscope.
terms.scienceExplanation: Microorganisms are organisms such as bacteria and many single-celled protists. They live in soil, water, air, and inside other organisms.
terms.contextExample: Microorganisms in the soil help break down fallen leaves.

terms.studentDefinition: An animal that eats plants.
terms.scienceExplanation: Herbivores are consumers that get their energy from producers. In a food chain, they usually come right after the plants.
terms.contextExample: A grasshopper eating grass is acting as a herbivore.

terms.studentDefinition: An animal that eats other animals.
terms.scienceExplanation: Carnivores are consumers that get their energy by eating other consumers. Energy in a food chain passes to them from the animals they eat.
terms.contextExample: A snake that eats frogs is a carnivore.

parts.meaning: a small animal with six legs

terms.studentDefinition: An animal that eats insects.
terms.scienceExplanation: Insectivores are a kind of carnivore. Naming what an animal eats helps explain its place in a food web.
terms.contextExample: A bat that catches moths at night is an insectivore.

terms.studentDefinition: A natural shape or feature of Earth's surface.
terms.scienceExplanation: Landforms such as mountains, valleys, canyons, and deltas are shaped over time by processes including weathering, erosion, and deposition.
terms.contextExample: A river slows near the coast and drops sediment, building a delta — a landform made by moving water.

terms.studentDefinition: To change from one form into another.
terms.scienceExplanation: In science, energy transforms from one form to another — for example, electrical energy transforms into light and thermal energy in a bulb.
terms.contextExample: When the bulb lights up, electrical energy transforms into light energy and thermal energy.

terms.studentDefinition: The same all the way through.
terms.scienceExplanation: Uniform describes something that does not vary — a uniform mixture looks the same in every sample you take from it.
terms.contextExample: After stirring, the salt water looked uniform — no grains settled at the bottom.

terms.studentDefinition: Heat that comes from inside Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: Geothermal energy is thermal energy stored in Earth's interior. It heats underground rock and water, and in some places it can be used to warm buildings or generate electricity.
terms.contextExample: In Iceland, hot water from underground is piped into homes for heating.

terms.studentDefinition: Electricity made by moving water.
terms.scienceExplanation: In a hydroelectric plant, falling or flowing water turns a turbine, and that motion is used to generate electricity. It is a renewable resource.
terms.contextExample: Water released from behind a dam spins turbines that generate hydroelectric power.

terms.studentDefinition: To use a material again instead of throwing it away.
terms.scienceExplanation: Recycling returns materials such as aluminum, glass, and paper to be processed and used again, which conserves natural resources.
terms.contextExample: The class recycled aluminum cans so the metal could be melted and shaped into something new.

terms.studentDefinition: The continuous movement of water on Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: Energy from the Sun drives evaporation. Water vapor rises, cools, and condenses into clouds, then returns to the surface as precipitation, and the pattern repeats.
terms.contextExample: A puddle shrinks on a sunny day. Later, clouds form and rain falls nearby.

terms.studentDefinition: The stages a living thing goes through from beginning to adult.
terms.scienceExplanation: A life cycle describes the sequence of stages an organism passes through, and it repeats when the adult produces offspring.
terms.contextExample: The life cycle of a butterfly moves from egg to larva to pupa to adult.

terms.studentDefinition: A resource that can be replaced in a short time.
terms.scienceExplanation: Renewable resources such as sunlight, wind, and moving water are replenished naturally on a human timescale. Nonrenewable resources such as coal are not.
terms.contextExample: A town compares a wind farm with a natural-gas plant and notes that only one uses a renewable resource.

terms.studentDefinition: Made of many cells.
terms.scienceExplanation: Multicellular organisms are built from many cells that work together, often with different cells doing different jobs.
terms.contextExample: An oak tree is multicellular: its leaf cells, root cells, and stem cells do different jobs.

terms.studentDefinition: Made of only one cell.
terms.scienceExplanation: A unicellular organism carries out all its life processes inside a single cell.
terms.contextExample: Many of the tiny moving organisms in pond water are unicellular.

terms.studentDefinition: In the form of a gas.
terms.scienceExplanation: Gaseous names one state of matter. In the gaseous state, particles are far apart and the material has no fixed shape or volume.
terms.contextExample: When water boils, liquid water becomes gaseous water vapor.

terms.studentDefinition: The layer of soil under the topsoil.
terms.scienceExplanation: Subsoil sits beneath topsoil. It usually holds less decayed plant material and more clay or small rock pieces.
terms.contextExample: The soil sample showed dark topsoil above a lighter, rockier subsoil.

terms.studentDefinition: Having to do with flight in the air and in space.
terms.scienceExplanation: Aerospace covers engineering and science for vehicles that travel through the atmosphere and beyond it.
terms.contextExample: An aerospace engineer tests how a model rocket moves through air before it leaves the atmosphere.

terms.studentDefinition: The study of objects in space.
terms.scienceExplanation: Astronomy studies the Sun, Moon, planets, stars, and their patterns of motion.
terms.contextExample: Recording the Moon's shape every night for a month is doing astronomy.

terms.studentDefinition: To say what you think will happen before it happens.
terms.scienceExplanation: A scientific prediction is based on evidence and on patterns you have already observed, not on a guess.
terms.contextExample: After watching shadows shrink all morning, students predicted the shortest shadow would come near noon.

terms.studentDefinition: The jelly-like fluid that fills a cell and holds its parts.
terms.scienceExplanation: Cytoplasm is the fluid inside a cell, outside the nucleus, where many of the cell's activities happen and where the organelles sit.
terms.contextExample: Under a microscope, the organelles of a cell appear to float in the cytoplasm.

terms.studentDefinition: The green substance in plants that captures light for photosynthesis.
terms.scienceExplanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment inside a plant's chloroplasts. It absorbs light energy, which the plant uses to make sugar during photosynthesis.
terms.contextExample: Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light and absorbs the rest.

terms.studentDefinition: A living thing that makes its own food.
terms.scienceExplanation: An autotroph, such as a green plant, makes its own food from simple materials using an energy source like sunlight. Autotrophs form the base of most food chains.
terms.contextExample: A blade of grass is an autotroph; it builds sugar from sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide.

terms.studentDefinition: A living thing that gets food by eating other living things.
terms.scienceExplanation: A heterotroph cannot make its own food, so it takes in food by eating autotrophs or other heterotrophs. Animals, fungi, and many microorganisms are heterotrophs.
terms.contextExample: A rabbit is a heterotroph; it must eat plants to get the energy it needs.

terms.studentDefinition: A change that takes in heat from its surroundings.
terms.scienceExplanation: In an endothermic process, energy is absorbed from the surroundings, so the surroundings feel colder. An instant cold pack that gets cold when squeezed is endothermic.
terms.contextExample: When the salt dissolves in an instant cold pack, the pack feels cold because the change is endothermic.

terms.studentDefinition: A change that gives off heat to its surroundings.
terms.scienceExplanation: In an exothermic process, energy is released to the surroundings, so they feel warmer. Burning fuel and many hand-warmer reactions are exothermic.
terms.contextExample: A hand warmer feels hot because the reaction inside it is exothermic.

terms.studentDefinition: The solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth.
terms.scienceExplanation: The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer shell — the crust and the upper part of the mantle. It is broken into the tectonic plates that move slowly over time.
terms.contextExample: Earthquakes happen where the plates of the lithosphere grind past one another.

terms.studentDefinition: Atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons.
terms.scienceExplanation: Isotopes are atoms of one element that share the same number of protons but differ in neutrons, so they have different masses. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon.
terms.contextExample: Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope that scientists use to estimate the age of old bones.

terms.studentDefinition: Located or happening inside a cell.
terms.scienceExplanation: Intracellular means within a single cell. The intracellular fluid is the cytoplasm and other fluid held inside the cell membrane.
terms.contextExample: Digestion that happens inside a cell is called intracellular digestion.

terms.studentDefinition: Located or happening between cells.
terms.scienceExplanation: Intercellular means between cells. Intercellular spaces are the gaps between cells, and intercellular signals pass from one cell to another.
terms.contextExample: Water can move through the intercellular spaces between the cells of a leaf.

terms.studentDefinition: Breaking a substance apart using water.
terms.scienceExplanation: In hydrolysis, a water molecule splits a larger molecule into smaller pieces. Digestion uses hydrolysis to break large food molecules into ones the body can absorb.
terms.contextExample: During digestion, hydrolysis breaks a starch molecule into separate sugar units.

terms.studentDefinition: A large molecule made of many repeating units.
terms.scienceExplanation: A polymer is built from many small units, called monomers, linked into a long chain. Plastics, proteins, and starch are polymers.
terms.contextExample: A plastic bottle is made of a polymer — thousands of identical units joined in chains.

terms.studentDefinition: A single small unit that can join with others to form a polymer.
terms.scienceExplanation: A monomer is one building-block molecule. When many monomers bond together, they form a polymer.
terms.contextExample: A single sugar unit is a monomer; many of them link together to form the polymer starch.

terms.studentDefinition: The same throughout, with parts you cannot pick out.
terms.scienceExplanation: A homogeneous mixture looks the same everywhere and its parts are evenly blended, like salt fully dissolved in water. You cannot see the separate ingredients.
terms.contextExample: Salt water is a homogeneous mixture; every sip tastes equally salty.

terms.studentDefinition: Made of parts you can still tell apart.
terms.scienceExplanation: A heterogeneous mixture has parts that are not evenly blended, so you can see or separate the different pieces, like sand in water or a salad.
terms.contextExample: A bowl of trail mix is a heterogeneous mixture; you can pick out the raisins from the nuts.

terms.studentDefinition: The lightest element; it can combine with oxygen to form water.
terms.scienceExplanation: Hydrogen is the lightest and most common element in the universe. Its name means 'water-producer' because burning hydrogen in oxygen makes water.
terms.contextExample: When hydrogen burns in air, the only product is water.

terms.studentDefinition: Letting some things pass through but not others.
terms.scienceExplanation: A semipermeable membrane lets certain particles pass while blocking others. A cell membrane is semipermeable, controlling what enters and leaves the cell.
terms.contextExample: Water passes through the semipermeable cell membrane, but larger molecules are held back.

terms.studentDefinition: The process of a liquid changing into a gas.
terms.scienceExplanation: Evaporation happens when particles at the surface of a liquid gain enough energy to escape as a gas. It happens faster when the liquid is warmer.
terms.contextExample: A puddle disappears on a warm day because the water undergoes evaporation.

terms.studentDefinition: The energy an object has because it is moving.
terms.scienceExplanation: Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving object. It grows when the object moves faster or has more mass, and it is zero when the object is at rest.
terms.contextExample: A rolling bowling ball has kinetic energy; the same ball sitting still has none.

terms.studentDefinition: A thread-like structure of coiled DNA that carries genes.
terms.scienceExplanation: A chromosome is a long molecule of DNA wound with protein. It was named a 'coloured body' because it absorbs dye. Human body cells carry 46 chromosomes, each holding many genes.
terms.contextExample: Before a cell divides, each chromosome is copied so both new cells receive a full set.

terms.studentDefinition: Relating to DNA and RNA, the acids concentrated in the nucleus.
terms.scienceExplanation: Nucleic acids — DNA and RNA — store and carry genetic information. They take their name from the cell nucleus, where they are concentrated.
terms.contextExample: DNA is the nucleic acid that carries the instructions for building proteins.

terms.studentDefinition: Cell division that produces two genetically identical cells.
terms.scienceExplanation: Mitosis is the process in which a cell divides into two cells with identical chromosomes. The chromosomes appear as threads during division, which is how the process was named.
terms.contextExample: A skin cell heals a cut by mitosis, making new cells identical to the original.

terms.studentDefinition: Cell division that halves the chromosome number to make sex cells.
terms.scienceExplanation: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number by half, producing gametes (egg and sperm). When two gametes join at fertilization, the full number is restored.
terms.contextExample: Meiosis makes sperm and egg cells with 23 chromosomes each, so a fertilized cell has 46.

terms.studentDefinition: Splitting a glucose molecule to release energy.
terms.scienceExplanation: Glycolysis is the first stage of cellular respiration. It splits one glucose molecule into smaller molecules, releasing a small amount of usable energy.
terms.contextExample: During exercise, muscle cells run glycolysis to release energy quickly from glucose.

terms.studentDefinition: The main sugar that cells break down for energy.
terms.scienceExplanation: Glucose is a simple sugar and the primary energy source for most cells. Its -OSE ending marks it as a sugar.
terms.contextExample: Blood carries glucose to cells, which break it down to release energy.

terms.studentDefinition: The set of alleles an organism carries for a trait.
terms.scienceExplanation: The genotype is an organism's genetic makeup — the combination of alleles it carries, such as Bb — whether or not those genes are visible.
terms.contextExample: A pea plant with the genotype Bb carries one dominant and one recessive allele.

terms.studentDefinition: The observable traits an organism actually shows.
terms.scienceExplanation: The phenotype is the set of visible characteristics of an organism, produced by its genotype interacting with the environment.
terms.contextExample: Two pea plants with genotypes BB and Bb can share the same purple-flower phenotype.

terms.studentDefinition: Keeping a stable internal state despite outside change.
terms.scienceExplanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a steady internal environment — such as body temperature or blood-sugar level — as conditions outside change.
terms.contextExample: When you get hot, sweating cools you down, keeping body temperature near 37 °C through homeostasis.

terms.studentDefinition: The sugar found in DNA.
terms.scienceExplanation: Deoxyribose is the sugar in DNA. Its name shows it is a ribose sugar with one fewer oxygen atom; the 'D' in DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic.
terms.contextExample: The backbone of a DNA strand is built from deoxyribose sugar and phosphate groups.

terms.studentDefinition: The sugar found in milk.
terms.scienceExplanation: Lactose is the sugar in milk. Its -OSE ending marks it as a sugar; the enzyme lactase breaks it down.
terms.contextExample: Milk tastes faintly sweet because it contains the sugar lactose.

terms.studentDefinition: The enzyme that breaks down the milk sugar lactose.
terms.scienceExplanation: Lactase is an enzyme that breaks lactose into smaller sugars the body can absorb. People who make little lactase are lactose intolerant.
terms.contextExample: An adult who makes little lactase cannot fully digest the lactose in a glass of milk.

terms.studentDefinition: A compound with one oxygen atom joined to another element.
terms.scienceExplanation: In a monoxide, a single oxygen atom is bonded to another element. Carbon monoxide (CO) has one carbon and one oxygen.
terms.contextExample: Carbon monoxide (CO) is dangerous because it carries only one oxygen and binds tightly to blood.

terms.studentDefinition: A compound with two oxygen atoms joined to another element.
terms.scienceExplanation: In a dioxide, two oxygen atoms are bonded to one atom of another element. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) has one carbon and two oxygens.
terms.contextExample: You breathe out carbon dioxide (CO₂); the DI- tells you it carries two oxygens, one more than monoxide.

terms.studentDefinition: A polyatomic ion of sulfur with four oxygens (SO₄²⁻).
terms.scienceExplanation: Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) is a polyatomic ion of sulfur and oxygen. The -ATE ending marks it as the oxygen-richer partner of sulfite.
terms.contextExample: Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate; the -ATE ending signals the oxygen-rich form.

terms.studentDefinition: A polyatomic ion of sulfur with three oxygens (SO₃²⁻).
terms.scienceExplanation: Sulfite (SO₃²⁻) has one fewer oxygen than sulfate. The -ITE ending marks the oxygen-poorer partner of the pair.
terms.contextExample: Dried fruit often lists sulfites as a preservative; the -ITE ending signals the oxygen-poorer form.

terms.studentDefinition: Using an electric current to split a compound into simpler parts.
terms.scienceExplanation: Electrolysis passes an electric current through a substance to break it apart, such as splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen gas.
terms.contextExample: Passing electricity through water by electrolysis releases hydrogen at one electrode and oxygen at the other.

terms.studentDefinition: One of two compounds with the same formula but a different arrangement.
terms.scienceExplanation: Isomers share an identical molecular formula but differ in how the atoms are arranged, so they can behave differently. Glucose and fructose are isomers (both C₆H₁₂O₆).
terms.contextExample: Glucose and fructose are isomers: same formula C₆H₁₂O₆, different structures and different sweetness.

terms.studentDefinition: A reaction that combines substances into a single product.
terms.scienceExplanation: In a synthesis (combination) reaction, two or more reactants join to form one more complex product, such as iron and sulfur forming iron sulfide.
terms.contextExample: When hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water, that is a synthesis reaction.

terms.studentDefinition: A reaction that breaks one compound into simpler substances.
terms.scienceExplanation: In a decomposition reaction, a single compound breaks into two or more simpler substances — the reverse of synthesis.
terms.contextExample: Heating hydrogen peroxide until it breaks into water and oxygen is a decomposition reaction.
